title: Beta users keep calling the new dashboard "confusing"
summary: Nineteen people used the same word about a redesign. The word is not the finding, and the survey that produced it has a problem.

brief.role: You are the PM for the analytics area of the product.
brief.company: Coreline, a 120-person company selling inventory software to mid-size retailers.
brief.context: Six weeks ago the team put a redesigned analytics dashboard into beta with 240 opted-in customers. The old dashboard was a wall of 22 metric tiles; the new one leads with four headline numbers and hides the rest behind a 'More metrics' expander. The in-beta survey has 47 responses and the word 'confusing' appears in 19 of the 31 free-text comments. The design lead reads this as 'we need to explain the new layout better' and has proposed an onboarding tour. The engineering lead reads it as 'we hid things people need'. General availability is scheduled in four weeks.
brief.objective: Work out what the feedback actually means before the team spends its remaining four weeks on the wrong fix.
brief.constraints: Four weeks to GA. One designer and two engineers. The researcher has two days available this week and none next week.
brief.task: Decide what the team does next and justify it from the evidence.

evidenceCards.title: Beta survey results
evidenceCards.content:
47 responses from 240 beta users (20% response rate).
Question: 'How would you describe the new dashboard?' (free text, 31 answered)

19 comments contain 'confusing' or 'confused'. Reading them, they split:
- 11 are about finding metrics: 'confusing where my stock turn number went', 'I can't find shrinkage', 'confusing, half the numbers are gone'.
- 5 are about the headline four: 'confusing which four you picked and why', 'the big numbers aren't the ones I care about'.
- 3 are general: 'looks nice but confusing', 'confusing at first, fine now'.

12 comments are positive, mostly about speed and the cleaner look.

Survey caveat noted by the researcher: the survey was emailed to all 240, but a banner prompting it was also shown inside the new dashboard, which means users who opened the dashboard and struggled were more likely to see the prompt.

evidenceCards.title: Beta usage data
evidenceCards.content:
Across the 240 beta users over six weeks:
- 'More metrics' expander opened at least once by 78% of users; opened in 61% of all sessions.
- Median time to first metric interaction: 9 seconds on the new dashboard, 21 seconds on the old one.
- Sessions per user per week: 4.1 new vs 3.6 old (same users, before and after).
- Of the four headline metrics, one — 'Units on hand' — is interacted with in 6% of sessions. The other three are between 34% and 51%.
- 14 of the 240 have asked support to be moved back to the old dashboard. All 14 are from the same customer segment: multi-location retailers with more than 20 stores.

evidenceCards.title: Interview notes
evidenceCards.content:
The researcher ran six 30-minute sessions two weeks ago, before the survey closed.
- Four single-location or small-chain users: all found their metrics within the expander after a few seconds and preferred the new layout. One said 'it was confusing the first day and then it wasn't'.
- Two multi-location users (12 and 34 stores): both struggled. Their workflow is to compare the same metric across stores, and the new dashboard shows company-wide totals in the headline with per-store data three clicks deep. One said 'this is built for someone who runs one shop'.
- Researcher's summary: 'I think we have two different jobs here, not one confusing layout. I would want more multi-location sessions before I'd stand behind that.'

evidenceCards.title: Design and delivery note
evidenceCards.content:
From the design lead and engineering lead:
- An onboarding tour highlighting the expander: three days, mostly design.
- Making the four headline metrics user-configurable: eight days, and it removes the 'why these four' complaint at the cost of the opinionated default.
- A per-store comparison view in the headline area for multi-location accounts: about three weeks, and it is a different layout, not a tweak.
- Multi-location accounts are 11% of beta users but 40% of revenue in this product area.
- GA can slip by two weeks without breaking any external commitment. Slipping further collides with the annual retail peak, during which the team ships nothing.

decisionPrompt: What should the team do in the four weeks before GA?

decisionOptions.label: Build the onboarding tour
decisionOptions.description: Treat the feedback as a discoverability problem and spend three days on a tour that highlights the 'More metrics' expander before GA.
decisionOptions.consequence:
The tour ships in four days and GA happens on schedule. Post-GA survey mentions of 'confusing' drop by about a third.
Multi-location complaints do not change at all — those users could already find the expander; their problem is the workflow underneath it. Three more large accounts ask to be moved back within a month, and the account team escalates. The per-store view starts in the following quarter, after peak.
Trade-off: you fixed the cheapest, most visible slice of the feedback and left the segment that carries 40% of revenue unaddressed for a quarter.
decisionOptions.rubricNote: Partial credit: the tour does address the 3 general and some of the 11 'where did it go' comments. Loses credit when the rationale treats one word as one problem and never segments the responses.

decisionOptions.label: Split the feedback by segment and use the researcher's two days on multi-location users
decisionOptions.description: Read the 19 comments as three different problems, spend the researcher's remaining two days on multi-location sessions, and decide scope for GA from that.
decisionOptions.consequence:
Five more multi-location sessions in two days confirm the pattern clearly: the job is cross-store comparison, and the new headline actively removes it.
The team ships configurable headline metrics in eight days, which lets multi-location users pin per-store views into the headline, and slips GA by one week. 'Confusing' mentions in the post-GA survey drop by about half, and the multi-location move-back requests stop.
The deeper per-store comparison view goes on the roadmap for after peak, now specified from evidence rather than argument.
Trade-off: you spent two days and a week of schedule to avoid building the wrong thing, and you still have not fully solved the multi-location workflow.
decisionOptions.rubricNote: Strongest when the rationale disaggregates the 19 comments, spots the multi-location signal in both usage data and interviews, and treats the survey's self-selection caveat correctly.

decisionOptions.label: Revert to the old dashboard before GA
decisionOptions.description: Nineteen of thirty-one comments is a strong negative signal. Pull the redesign back and rethink.
decisionOptions.consequence:
Beta users are moved back. The 14 multi-location accounts are relieved; a larger number of small-chain users complain, since sessions per user were up and time-to-first-metric was down for them.
The redesign is reopened in the following quarter with no clearer brief than before, because the team never separated the two jobs. Peak passes with the old 22-tile dashboard in place.
Trade-off: you responded decisively to a loud signal and discarded measured improvements for the majority of users.
decisionOptions.rubricNote: Weak. The usage data shows the redesign is working for most users; reverting on an unsegmented word count ignores it. Only credit if the rationale somehow engages with and rebuts the usage evidence.

decisionOptions.label: Ship configurable headline metrics and go to GA
decisionOptions.description: Spend the eight days making the four headline metrics user-configurable, which answers the 'why these four' complaint directly, and hold the GA date.
decisionOptions.consequence:
Configurable headlines ship in nine days and GA slips by three days. The 'which four and why' complaints disappear and 'Units on hand', used in 6% of sessions, is swapped out by most users.
Multi-location users can now pin metrics they care about but still cannot compare across stores in the headline, so about half of the move-back requests persist. The account team is partly satisfied.
Trade-off: a solid fix aimed at the second-largest cluster of feedback, chosen without checking whether the largest cluster was the same problem.
decisionOptions.rubricNote: Good instinct and a real fix, but the rationale should acknowledge it was chosen without segmenting first. Higher credit when it names the multi-location risk and schedules the research anyway.

rubric.referenceReasoning: Nineteen people using the same word is not nineteen people reporting the same problem. Reading the comments splits them into at least three groups: 'I cannot find my metric' (11), 'you picked the wrong four' (5), and 'unfamiliar at first' (3). The usage data argues against a general usability failure — 78% found the expander, time to first metric halved, sessions per user rose. It also points at the real cluster: every move-back request comes from multi-location retailers, who are 11% of beta users and 40% of revenue, and the interviews explain why — their job is cross-store comparison and the new headline removed it. The survey is also self-selected toward frustrated users because of the in-product banner. So the right move is to disaggregate before deciding, spend the researcher's two remaining days on the segment that matters, and choose scope from that. A strong answer treats 'confusing' as a symptom to be decomposed, not a finding.
evidenceSignals: Splits the 19 'confusing' comments into distinct underlying problems
Notices that all 14 move-back requests come from multi-location retailers
Uses the usage data (78% expander use, faster time to first metric, more sessions) as counter-evidence to a general usability failure
Recognises the in-dashboard survey banner biases responses toward frustrated users
Weighs 11% of users against 40% of revenue in that product area

product_sense: Identifies that two different jobs are being served by one layout
Notices 'Units on hand' at 6% usage is a weak headline choice
analytics: Uses behavioural data to test what the qualitative feedback claims
Reads the response rate and self-selection as limits on what the survey can support
user_research: Treats a repeated word as a symptom and decomposes it
Targets the remaining research time at the segment where the signal is strongest
Respects the researcher's own caveat about sample size
prioritization: Trades a one-week GA slip against building the wrong fix
Sequences the cheap configurable change ahead of the three-week rebuild
execution: Notes the peak-season window as a hard constraint on later work
communication: Gives the design and engineering leads a specific reason both readings were partly right

product_sense: Treats the redesign as simply good or simply bad rather than good for one job and bad for another
analytics: Counts word frequency and stops there
Ignores the usage data that contradicts a general usability problem
user_research: Takes 19 of 31 as a representative measure of 240 users
Ignores the self-selection introduced by the in-product survey prompt
prioritization: Commits to the three-week rebuild with four weeks to GA and peak season behind it
communication: Presents 'users are confused' as the finding rather than a starting point

learnTakeaway.title: A repeated word is a symptom, not a finding
learnTakeaway.body: When many users describe a product with the same adjective, the useful work starts after you notice it: read each comment for the underlying job, then check whether behaviour agrees. 'Confusing' can mean 'I cannot find it', 'you chose wrong', or 'it is new'. Those have different fixes and different costs. Segmenting by who said it — especially when one segment carries disproportionate revenue — usually turns a vague complaint into a specific, buildable problem.

qaSubmissions.label: strong
qaSubmissions.rationale: One word is hiding three problems: 11 comments are 'I can't find my metric', 5 are 'you picked the wrong four', 3 are 'new at first'. And behaviour argues against a general usability failure — 78% found the expander, time to first metric halved, sessions rose. The real signal is segment-shaped: all 14 move-back requests are multi-location retailers, 11% of beta users and 40% of revenue, and their job is comparing a metric across stores. I'd also discount the survey: the in-product banner over-samples frustrated users. Spend the researcher's two days on multi-location sessions, then set scope.

qaSubmissions.label: defensible_alternative
qaSubmissions.rationale: Ship configurable headline metrics and hold GA. The behavioural data says the redesign is working — expander use 78%, time to first metric 21s to 9s, sessions up — so I don't want to slow a redesign that's broadly succeeding. Configurability answers the sharpest specific complaint, fixes an error we can already see (Units on hand at 6% of sessions), and helps every segment somewhat. The honest gap: I'm choosing without segmenting the 19 comments, and the multi-location move-backs suggest a workflow problem this won't solve. So I'd run the researcher's two days in parallel.

qaSubmissions.label: weak
qaSubmissions.rationale: 19 out of 31 comments say the dashboard is confusing, which is over 60%, so discoverability is clearly the main issue. An onboarding tour is only three days and would show people where the More metrics expander is, so we can still hit GA on time.
